cards.q: What is VLSM and what is its core idea?
cards.a: Variable-Length Subnet Masking divides a single address space into subnets with different prefix lengths so each is sized to its actual host requirement; the core idea is to give each subnet only as much address space as it needs, improving IPv4 utilization compared with fixed-length subnet masking (FLSM).

FLSM uses the same mask on every subnet (e.g. all /26), is simpler to plan, but can waste addresses; VLSM uses a different mask per subnet (e.g. /26, /27, /28, /30), is more efficient, but requires careful planning and a classless routing protocol to advertise the variable prefixes.

cards.q: Allocate VLSM subnets for 50, 25, 10, and 2 hosts from 10.10.0.0/24.
What is the VLSM sizing rule and quick formula?
cards.a: Reserve network + usable hosts + broadcast, so 2^h ≥ hosts required + 2, then prefix = 32 − h; the quick formula is hosts + 2, take the next power of 2 as the block size, and prefix = 32 − log2(block size).

cards.q: Give the block size and prefix for 2, 6, 10, 14, 25, 30, 50, 62, 126, and 254 hosts.
How do you determine valid subnet block boundaries?

cards.a: No; a /27 has a block size of 32, so its network addresses must be multiples of 32 such as .0, .32, .64, .96; .80 is not a valid network boundary, whereas 10.10.0.64/27 is valid.

cards.q: What is the difference between VLSM and route summarization?
cards.a: VLSM divides an address space using different prefix lengths, whereas summarization combines multiple contiguous routes into a shorter prefix; for example four contiguous /26s from 10.10.0.0/26 to 10.10.0.192/26 summarize to 10.10.0.0/24, but a summary must cover the intended networks without accidentally including unrelated ones.

cards.q: Why does VLSM require a classless routing protocol and which protocols support it?
cards.a: Because the routing protocol must carry the subnet mask/prefix length with each route; RIPv2, OSPF, EIGRP, IS-IS, and BGP are classless and support VLSM, while RIPv1 is classful and cannot properly advertise variable subnetting information.

cards.q: Which routing protocol cannot support VLSM and why?
cards.a: RIPv1, because it does not advertise the subnet mask in its updates; RIPv2 and the other classless protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, IS-IS, BGP) do support VLSM.

cards.q: How do you configure VLSM on Cisco IOS?
cards.a: No special command is needed; configure each interface with the appropriate mask, e.g. Vlan10 ip address 10.10.0.1 255.255.255.192 (/26), Vlan20 ip address 10.10.0.65 255.255.255.224 (/27), Serial0/0 ip address 10.10.0.113 255.255.255.252 (/30); the interface IP must be a usable host address, not the network or broadcast.

cards.q: What is the VLSM planning procedure for exam questions?
cards.a: Identify the available address space; list all host requirements; sort from largest to smallest; calculate each subnet size; allocate sequentially at correct boundaries; then verify host capacity, network boundaries, no overlap, broadcast addresses, usable ranges, and remaining space.

cards.q: Why should you always allocate the largest host requirements first in VLSM?
cards.a: Sorting requirements from largest to smallest reduces fragmentation and makes VLSM planning and sequential allocation much easier.

cards.q: Why is it a trap to forget the +2 when sizing a subnet?
cards.a: Traditional subnetting requires hosts + 1 network + 1 broadcast, so 50 hosts needs 52 addresses, which needs a 64-address block (/26); forgetting +2 gives a block too small to address the network and broadcast.

cards.q: Why is 10.10.0.100/28 invalid as a network, and does 10.10.0.32/27 overlap 10.10.0.0/26?
cards.a: A /28 has block size 16, so valid networks are .0, .16, .32, .48, .64, .80, .96, .112..., making .100 invalid. And 10.10.0.32/27 lies inside the 10.10.0.0/26 range, so it overlaps; the correct neighbor is 10.10.0.64/27.

cards.q: Is a /30 the only option for point-to-point links?
cards.a: No; /30 (4 addresses, 2 usable) is the traditional point-to-point choice, but modern point-to-point links can also use /31, which provides two addresses and is specifically designed for point-to-point links.

cards.q: State the VLSM recall chain from smaller to larger subnets.
cards.a: 2 hosts = /30, 6 hosts = /29, 14 hosts = /28, 30 hosts = /27, 62 hosts = /26, 126 hosts = /25, 254 hosts = /24.

cards.q: What is the core VLSM mental model?
cards.a: Host requirement → add network and broadcast → choose the next power-of-2 block → calculate the prefix → place it at the correct boundary → repeat from largest to smallest requirement; the key exam rule is largest first, correct alignment, and no overlap.
